title: Tracking basics
summary: How a click becomes a number you can trust: UTMs, click IDs, pixels, the Conversions API, postbacks and attribution windows. By the end you can build a simple tracking setup and explain why your ad platform and your network never show exactly the same numbers.

lessons.title: Why tracking decides everything
objectives: By the end you can explain what tracking is in one sentence.
By the end you can list the steps between an ad view and a deposit.
By the end you can name the three places your numbers come from.

steps.p: When you run ads, money leaves your account every hour. Tracking is the system that tells you which ad, which audience and which creative brought back a real result. Without it you are guessing, and guessing with a budget gets expensive very quickly.

d.s: You cannot fix what you cannot see

steps.say: When you run ads, money leaves your account every hour. Tracking is the system that tells you which ad, which audience and which creative brought back a real result. Without it, you're guessing, and guessing with a budget gets expensive very quickly. No tracking, no decisions. You can't fix what you can't see.

steps.p: Every conversion is a chain of small events. A person sees your ad, clicks it, lands on a page, signs up with the advertiser and maybe deposits days later. Tracking means recording each link in that chain and tying it back to the ad that started it.
steps.more: Notice that the first three steps happen on the ad platform and your page, while the last two happen on the advertiser's website. That split is the whole reason tracking feels hard at first. You need a way to carry a label from your ad all the way to the advertiser, then get the result back. The rest of this module is about building that bridge.
steps.say: Every conversion is a chain of small events. Follow the flow on screen. A person sees your ad, clicks it, lands on a page, signs up with the advertiser, and maybe deposits days later. Notice the split. The first three steps happen on the ad platform and your page. The last two happen on the advertiser's website. That's why tracking feels hard at first. You need to carry a label from your ad to the advertiser, then get the result back. This module builds that bridge.

steps.p: A good setup answers three questions for every conversion. If you cannot answer all three for a sale or a deposit, your tracking has a gap somewhere and your decisions will be weaker.
d: Where|which source, campaign, ad set and ad
What|which action happened: sign-up, FTD, deposit
How much|what that action paid you
steps.say: A good setup answers three questions for every conversion. Look at the cards. Where: which source, campaign, ad set and ad. What: which action happened, a sign-up, an F T D, meaning a first time deposit, or another deposit. And how much: what that action paid you. If you can't answer all three for a sale or a deposit, your tracking has a gap, and your decisions will be weaker.

steps.p: Two buyers can spend the same money and learn completely different things. The difference is not talent. It is whether they set up tracking before the first dollar went out.

a.title: Guessing
items: Scale the ad with most clicks
Blame the offer when it fails
Argue with the network over numbers

b.title: Tracking
items: Scale the ad with most deposits

steps.say: Two buyers can spend the same money and learn completely different things. On the left, guessing: scale the ad with the most clicks, blame the offer when it fails, can't repeat a good day, and argue with the network over numbers. On the right, tracking: scale the ad with the most deposits, see exactly where people drop, copy what worked on purpose, and match numbers to the click. The difference isn't talent. It's whether tracking was set up before the first dollar went out.

steps.p: Example: an ad sends 1,000 clicks. Only 820 load the landing page, 90 register and 9 make a first deposit. Each drop tells you something different, and you only see the drops if each step is recorded.
steps.more: Example figures. The gap between 1,000 clicks and 820 page views is common: some people tap by accident, some leave before a slow page loads, and some clicks come from bots. The gap from 820 to 90 is about your page and the offer. The gap from 90 to 9 is about lead quality and the advertiser's sign-up and deposit process. Three gaps, three different fixes.
steps.say: Here's a funnel in numbers. These are example figures. One thousand clicks. Only eight hundred and twenty load the landing page. Ninety register, and nine make a first deposit. Each drop tells you something different. Clicks to page views is about accidental taps, slow pages and bots. Page views to registrations is about your page and the offer. Registrations to deposits is about lead quality and the advertiser's process. Three gaps, three different fixes. And you only see them if each step is recorded.

steps.p: Example: two ad sets each spent $50. The ad platform says ad set A is the winner because it has more clicks. The network report, matched by click, tells a different story.
steps.more: Example. Cost per FTD is spend divided by FTDs. Ad set A: $50 ÷ 1 = $50 per FTD. Ad set B: $50 ÷ 4 = $12.50 per FTD. A buyer who only reads the ad platform would raise the budget on A and slowly lose money. A buyer with click-level tracking raises B and pauses A. Same spend, opposite decision.
steps.say: Here's a worked example. Two ad sets each spent fifty dollars. The ad platform says ad set A is the winner, because it has four hundred clicks against two hundred and twenty. But look at the F T D column, from the network report matched by click. A has one F T D. B has four. So A costs fifty dollars per F T D, and B costs twelve dollars fifty. A buyer reading only the platform would raise A and slowly lose money. With click-level tracking, you raise B and pause A. Same spend, opposite decision.

steps.h: The number that changes the decision
steps.p: Example: ad set B brings first deposits at $12.50 each, four times cheaper than ad set A. You only see this number when FTDs from the network are matched to the ad set that produced them.

d.label: cost per FTD for ad set B

steps.say: This is the number that changes the decision. Twelve dollars and fifty cents, the cost per F T D for ad set B. That's four times cheaper than ad set A. And you only see this number when F T Ds from the network are matched to the ad set that produced them. It's an example, so use your own numbers.

steps.p: You will read numbers from three places. Each sees part of the journey. Learning which one to trust for which question is a core skill for a media buyer.
d: Ad platform|spend, impressions, clicks, its own conversion count
Your tracker or sheet|joins them together by click
steps.say: You'll read numbers from three places, and each sees part of the journey. Look at the cards. The ad platform shows spend, impressions, clicks, and its own conversion count. The network or advertiser shows registrations, F T Ds and payouts. And your tracker or sheet joins them together by click. Learning which one to trust for which question is a core skill for a media buyer.

steps.h: Money is counted on the network side
steps.p: The ad platform reports what it believes happened. The network decides what you are actually paid. When the two disagree, the network report is the one that pays your bills, so it is the one you reconcile against.

d.s: Reconcile to the source of payment

steps.say: Here's the key idea. The ad platform reports what it believes happened. The network decides what you're actually paid. When the two disagree, the network report is the one that pays your bills, so that's the one you reconcile against. Platform guides, network pays.

steps.h: The tracking system on one page
steps.p: This is the whole system you will build. The click leaves your ad with labels attached, passes your page and reaches the advertiser. The network records the result against your click ID and reports it back. Your sheet joins spend and results by ad set.
steps.say: This map is the whole system you'll build. Follow the arrows. The click leaves your Meta ad with labels attached, called U T Ms, and reaches your lander. From there, a click I D travels in a sub ID slot to the advertiser's sign-up. The sign-up and F T D are recorded in the network report, which fires a postback. The postback sends F T Ds by ad set into your daily sheet. And spend comes straight from the ad into the same sheet, where spend and results are joined.

steps.h: Walkthrough: find your sub ID report
steps.p: Most networks have a report you can group by sub ID. Open your network dashboard, find the statistics or reports area and group by sub1 to sub3. Every network names this differently, so ask your manager if you cannot find it.

steps.h: What you must see before launch
steps.p: Before spending on any campaign, make sure you can see these numbers broken down by ad set and, ideally, by ad. If one is missing, fix it first.
steps.say: Before you spend on any campaign, make sure you can see these numbers broken down by ad set, and ideally by ad. Spend per ad set. Clicks per ad set. Registrations per ad set. F T Ds per ad set. And payout per F T D. If one is missing, fix it first.

steps.p: The Budget and kill rules module gives exact starting rules, such as kill an ad set at spend of 2 × target CPA with 0 network-confirmed FTDs. You can only apply a rule like that if each FTD is matched to the ad set that produced it.

d.text: Example: target CPA $25. Ad set A spent $50 and the network shows 0 FTDs for its sub ID. Starting rule: kill. Without sub IDs you could not tell which ad set had 0.

steps.say: The Budget and kill rules module gives exact starting rules, such as: kill an ad set at spend of two times target C P A, cost per acquisition, with zero network-confirmed F T Ds. You can only apply that if each F T D is matched to its ad set. Here's the example. Target C P A twenty five dollars. Ad set A spent fifty, and the network shows zero F T Ds for its sub ID. Starting rule: kill. Without sub IDs, you couldn't tell which ad set had zero.

steps.p: These four mistakes cost beginners the most money in their first month. Each one has a simple fix that takes minutes before launch, and each fix is taught in the lessons that follow.
d: Deciding on clicks|decide on network FTDs instead
Launching untested|send one test click first
One link for every ad set|fill sub IDs per ad set
Trusting one report|reconcile platform and network daily
steps.say: These four mistakes cost beginners the most money in their first month. Deciding on clicks: decide on network F T Ds instead. Launching untested: send one test click first. One link for every ad set: fill sub IDs per ad set. And trusting one report: reconcile platform and network daily. Each fix takes minutes before launch, and each one is taught in the lessons that follow.

steps.p: Running a test without tracking is like taking an exam and never getting the results back. You pay the full price and learn almost nothing you can use.

d.text: Do not launch until a test click shows up in both your ad platform and your network report.

steps.say: Running a test without tracking is like taking an exam and never getting the results back. You pay the full price and learn almost nothing you can use. So here's the warning on screen: don't launch until a test click shows up in both your ad platform and your network report.

Clicks are not results. Decide on registrations and deposits.
The network report is the money report. Reconcile against it.

quiz.q: What is the main job of tracking?
options: Linking each result back to the ad that caused it
quiz.why: Tracking connects results to their source so you can decide what to scale or pause. It does not change prices or approvals.

quiz.q: Ad set A: $50 spend, 1 FTD. Ad set B: $50 spend, 4 FTDs. What is B's cost per FTD?
quiz.why: $50 ÷ 4 = $12.50. Cost per FTD is spend divided by the number of FTDs.

quiz.q: Which report decides what you are actually paid?
quiz.why: The network pays you based on its own records, so it is the report you reconcile against.

quiz.q: 1,000 clicks became 820 page views. Which is NOT a likely reason for the gap?
quiz.why: Deposit rejections happen much later in the funnel. The click to page view gap is about loading, accidents and bots.

quiz.q: Which ad should you scale first?
options: The one with the most likes
The one with the cheapest clicks
The one with the most comments
The one with the lowest cost per FTD that pays out
quiz.why: Scale on results that earn money. Likes and cheap clicks can look good while returning nothing.

lessons.title: UTMs and click IDs
objectives: By the end you can read every part of a tracked link.
By the end you can write UTMs with a clean naming system.
By the end you can explain the difference between a UTM and a click ID.

steps.p: A URL parameter is extra information added to the end of a link after a question mark. The page still opens normally, but the label travels with the visitor so tools can read where they came from.

d.s: Parameters ride along at the end of the link

steps.say: A URL parameter is extra information added to the end of a link, after a question mark. The page still opens normally, but the label travels with the visitor, so tools can read where they came from. Every click carries a label. The parameters just ride along at the end of the link.

steps.p: Example link: example.com/start?utm_source=facebook&utm_medium=paid. Each part has a job. Once you can read these four parts, every tracking link you meet from now on will make sense.
steps.say: Let's take a tracked link apart. Look at the table. It has four parts, each with a job. The base U R L is the page that opens. The question mark is where parameters start. Then comes a key and value, like source equals facebook, which is one label. And the ampersand, the and sign, joins the next label. Once you can read these four parts, every tracking link you meet will make sense.

steps.p: UTM parameters are a common standard first made popular by Google Analytics. Most analytics tools read them. You choose the values yourself, so consistency matters more than the exact words.
steps.say: U T M parameters are a common standard, first made popular by Google Analytics, and most analytics tools read them. There are five. Look at the table. U T M source answers which site or app, like facebook. Medium answers what kind of traffic, like paid social. Campaign answers which campaign. Content answers which ad or creative, like video hook three. And term answers keyword or audience. You choose the values yourself, so consistency matters more than the exact words.

steps.p: Here is a complete tracked link for one ad. Read it left to right and you can tell the source, the campaign, the geo and the exact creative without opening Ads Manager.
steps.say: Here's a complete tracked link for one ad, shown on screen. I won't read it out, but read it left to right yourself. From the labels alone, you can tell the source is facebook, the medium is paid social, the campaign is a Kenya trading test, number one, and the creative is video hook three. All that, without opening Ads Manager.

steps.h: Naming rules that save you later
steps.p: Names you choose today become the filters you use for months. Messy names make reports useless. Pick a system now, write it down and use it on every campaign.
d: One letter case, used every time
Same order every time: geo, vertical, test
Add a test number: t1, t2, t3
Keep a naming key in your sheet
steps.more: Many buyers use lowercase for UTM values, because some analytics tools treat Kenya and kenya as two different sources. Campaign names in Ads Manager can use capitals, as in the First campaign module, as long as you use the same pattern every time.
steps.say: Names you choose today become the filters you use for months. Messy names make reports useless. So pick a system, write it down and use it everywhere. Look at the list. One letter case, used every time. No spaces, use underscores. The same order every time: geo, vertical, test. A test number, like t one, t two, t three. And a naming key in your sheet. Many buyers use lowercase for U T M values, because some tools treat Kenya with a capital K and kenya in lowercase as two different sources.

On the right, clean: k e trading t one, t two and t three. Only the clean column can be sorted, filtered and understood by a teammate, or by you, three months from now.

steps.h: UTMs label the group. Click IDs label the person.
steps.p: A UTM says this visitor came from campaign ke_trading_t1. A click ID is a unique code for one single click. It lets you match one click to one registration and one deposit.
steps.say: Here's an important difference. U T Ms label the group. Click I Ds label the person. A U T M says this visitor came from a certain campaign. A click I D is a unique code for one single click. It lets you match one click to one registration and one deposit. Group label versus single click. You need both.

steps.p: The click ID is created at the moment of the click and has to survive every hop. If any step drops it, the conversion arrives with no way to link it back to your ad.
steps.more: Two kinds of click ID exist side by side. The ad platform adds its own, such as fbclid on Meta clicks, which the platform uses for its own matching. Your tracker or the network creates a second one, often called click_id or sub ID, which you control. When you hear "pass the click ID", people usually mean the second one: put it in the offer link so the network can send it back to you with the conversion.
steps.say: The click I D is created at the moment of the click and has to survive every hop. Follow the flow. Click on the ad. A unique I D is created. The I D is added to the link. The advertiser saves it at sign-up. And the I D returns with the conversion. If any step drops it, the conversion has no way back to your ad. There are two kinds. The platform adds its own, like f b c l i d on Meta. Your tracker or network creates a second one, which you control. Pass the click I D usually means put that second one in the offer link.

steps.p: You do not need to memorise these, but you should recognise them in a URL. Names change over time and differ by platform and network, so check the current documentation.
d: fbclid|added by Meta to ad clicks
click_id or sub_id|created by your tracker or network
steps.say: You don't need to memorise these, but you should recognise them in a URL. Look at the cards. f b c l i d is added by Meta to ad clicks. g c l i d is added by Google Ads. t t c l i d is added by TikTok ads. And click I D or sub I D is created by your tracker or network. Names change over time and differ by platform and network, so check the current documentation.

steps.h: How the offer link carries your ID
steps.p: Networks give you an offer link with empty slots called sub IDs. You fill one slot with your click ID. When a conversion happens, the network reports that value back.
steps.more: Sub ID slot names vary: sub1, aff_sub, s1, subid and others. Many networks give you several slots. A simple pattern: sub1 = click ID, sub2 = campaign, sub3 = ad set, sub4 = ad. Even without a paid tracker, filling sub2 to sub4 lets you group network conversions by campaign and ad set inside the network's own report.
steps.say: Networks give you an offer link with empty slots called sub IDs. Look at the equation. Offer link, plus your click I D in sub one, equals a traceable conversion. When a conversion happens, the network reports that value back. Slot names vary, like sub one, aff sub, s one or subid. A simple pattern: sub one is the click I D, sub two the campaign, sub three the ad set, sub four the ad. Even without a paid tracker, filling sub two to four lets you group conversions inside the network's own report.

steps.p: Example: you put the ad set name in sub3. After two days the network report, grouped by sub3, shows this. The answer to which ad set to keep is now obvious.
steps.more: Example figures. Each ad set spent about the same. hook3 has the most registrations and the most FTDs, so it gets more budget. hook2 has 18 registrations but zero deposits, which can mean the angle attracts curious people who never intended to deposit. Without sub3 you would only see 70 registrations and 8 FTDs in total, with no idea where they came from.
steps.say: Here's a worked example. You put the ad set name in sub three, and after two days the network report, grouped by sub three, shows this. Hook three has the most registrations, thirty, and the most F T Ds, first time deposits, five. So it gets more budget. Hook two has eighteen registrations but zero deposits, which can mean the angle attracts curious people who never intended to deposit. Without sub three, you'd only see seventy registrations and eight F T Ds in total, with no idea where they came from.

steps.p: Most broken links come from a handful of small typing mistakes. Each one silently breaks tracking, so the ads still run and you only find out days later, when the network report is empty or grouped under one blank value.
d: A second ?|use & after the first one
Old link reused|rebuild it for each campaign
Empty sub IDs|test one click before spend
steps.say: Most broken links come from a few small typing mistakes. Look at the cards. A second question mark: use an ampersand after the first one. Spaces or mixed case: use lowercase with underscores. An old link reused: rebuild it for each campaign. Empty sub IDs: test one click before spend. Each one silently breaks tracking. The ads still run, and you only find out days later, when the network report is empty or grouped under one blank value.

steps.h: Compliance: no personal data in links
steps.p: Links are copied into logs, reports and analytics tools that many people can see. Ad platform terms usually forbid sending personal data in URLs, and privacy law in many countries limits it too.

d.text: Never put names, phone numbers, emails or ID numbers in UTMs or sub IDs. Use click IDs and campaign names only.

lessons.title: Pixels and the Conversions API
objectives: By the end you can explain what a pixel does and why platforms need it.
By the end you can describe how the Conversions API differs from a browser pixel.
By the end you can explain deduplication with an example.

steps.h: The pixel is the platform's eyes
steps.p: A pixel is a small piece of code on your web page. When someone loads the page or completes an action, it sends a message called an event back to the ad platform. Meta, TikTok, Snapchat and Google all have their own version.

d.s: From your page back to the ad platform

steps.say: A pixel is a small piece of code on your web page. When someone loads the page or completes an action, it sends a message called an event back to the ad platform. Think of it as the platform's eyes on your page. Meta, TikTok, Snapchat and Google all have their own version.

steps.p: Everything happens in the visitor's browser in a fraction of a second. The platform then tries to match the event to a person who saw or clicked your ad.
steps.say: Here's how a pixel event travels. Follow the flow. The page loads. The pixel code runs. An event is sent to the platform. The platform matches it to an ad click. And it's shown in reports. Everything happens in the visitor's browser, in a fraction of a second. Then the platform tries to match the event to a person who saw or clicked your ad.

steps.p: Platforms offer a menu of standard events. Pick the ones that match real steps in your funnel. Event names differ between platforms and change over time, so check the current list.
d: Purchase|someone paid; can carry a value
steps.say: Platforms offer a menu of standard events. Look at the cards. Page View, someone loaded the page. View Content, someone viewed key content. Lead, someone left contact details. Complete Registration, someone signed up. And Purchase, someone paid, which can carry a value. Pick the ones that match real steps in your funnel. Event names differ between platforms and change over time, so check the current list.

steps.h: What a standard event looks like
steps.p: Once the base pixel code is on your page, one line fires an event. This is the shape of Meta's browser call at the time of writing. You do not need to write it by hand yet; the point is to recognise it.

d.text:
// fires when the sign-up form is submitted
fbq('track', 'CompleteRegistration', {}, { eventID: 'reg_8812' });
d.note: Syntax at the time of writing; check Meta's developer docs. Full setup: Tracking setup lab module.

steps.say: Once the base pixel code is on your page, one line fires an event. The code on screen is the shape of Meta's browser call at the time of writing. It fires when the sign-up form is submitted, and it carries an event I D. You don't need to write it by hand yet. The point is to recognise it. Check Meta's developer docs for current syntax, and see the Tracking setup lab module for the full setup.

steps.p: Events are not only for reports. The platform's delivery system learns from them. If you tell it to find people who register, it studies who registered and shows your ad to more people like them.

d.s: The event you feed is the customer you get

steps.say: Events do two jobs: reporting and learning. They're not only for reports. The platform's delivery system learns from them. If you tell it to find people who register, it studies who registered and shows your ad to more people like them. So the event you feed is the customer you get.

steps.p: Events near the top of the funnel happen often but say little about money. Events near deposits say a lot but happen rarely. Bar length here shows how often each event happens in an example funnel.
steps.more: Example proportions, not a benchmark. The skill is choosing the deepest event that still happens often enough for the platform to learn. A beginner on a small budget often optimises for registrations first, while sending FTDs as a separate event so they can be reported and used later when volume grows.
steps.say: Look at the bars. They show how often each event happens in an example funnel, not a benchmark. Link clicks and page views happen a lot, but they're weak signals about money. Registrations are fewer, with a better signal. First deposits are rare, but the strongest signal. The skill is choosing the deepest event that still happens often enough for the platform to learn. On a small budget, beginners often optimise for registrations first, while sending F T Ds, first time deposits, as a separate event for later.

steps.h: Worked example: can it learn on FTDs?
steps.p: Example: $20 a day budget. Platforms need a steady flow of optimisation events to learn. At the time of writing, Meta's guidance has long been around 50 events per ad set per week. We are not certain it is current; check.
steps.more: Example. $20 × 7 days = $140 a week. At $4 per registration that is $140 ÷ 4 = 35 registrations a week. At $40 per FTD it is $140 ÷ 40 = 3.5 FTDs a week. Neither hits 50, but 35 registrations gives the system far more to learn from than 3.5 deposits. The learning threshold is a rough guide and it changes, so read the current help pages for your platform.
steps.say: Here's a worked example: a twenty dollar a day budget. That's one hundred and forty dollars a week. At four dollars per registration, you get thirty five registrations a week. At forty dollars per F T D, just three and a half. At the time of writing, Meta's guidance has long been around fifty events per ad set per week, but we're not certain it's current, so check. Neither hits fifty, but thirty five registrations give the system far more to learn from than three and a half deposits.

steps.p: A browser pixel depends on the visitor's phone and browser. Some block it, some clear cookies, and privacy features limit what it can see. Server events come from your server, not the browser.

a.title: Browser pixel
items: Only sees actions on your page

b.title: Server events (CAPI)
items: Sent from your server or tool
Can send off-site events like deposits

steps.say: Compare the two sides. A browser pixel runs on the visitor's device. Ad blockers can stop it, it only sees actions on your page, but it's quick to install. Server events, called C A P I, are sent from your server or tool. They're not stopped by browser blockers, and they can send off-site events like deposits, but they need more setup. The browser pixel depends on the visitor's phone and browser, and privacy features limit what it can see.

steps.h: The Conversions API in one line
steps.p: The Conversions API, often called CAPI, lets your server tell the ad platform directly that a conversion happened. Meta calls it the Conversions API. TikTok and Snapchat have their own versions with similar ideas.
steps.say: Here's the Conversions A P I in one line: your server tells the platform. It's often called C A P I. It lets your server tell the ad platform directly that a conversion happened, with no browser in the middle. Meta calls it the Conversions A P I. TikTok and Snapchat have their own versions with similar ideas.

steps.p: Server events are how deposits that happen on the advertiser's site, days after the click, can still reach Meta and help it learn who your best users are.
steps.more: For affiliates the usual path is: the network sends a postback to your tracker or tool, and the tool sends a server event to the ad platform. You will learn postbacks in the next lesson. Tools that sit in the middle, such as trackers or Joinvoo for Telegram funnels, exist to do this step for you without writing code.
steps.say: Server events are how deposits on the advertiser's site, days after the click, can still reach Meta and help it learn who your best users are. Follow the flow. A conversion happens. Your tool receives it. It sends an event plus click data. The platform matches it, then reports and learns. For affiliates, the usual path is: the network sends a postback to your tool, and the tool sends a server event. Tools in the middle, like trackers or Joinvoo for Telegram funnels, do this step without code.

steps.p: A server event is only useful if the platform can match it to someone who clicked your ad. These details improve matching. Send personal data only with consent and as the platform's rules require.
d: Click ID|such as the fbc value made from fbclid
Browser ID|such as the fbp value
Hashed contact data|email or phone, scrambled, with consent
steps.say: A server event is only useful if the platform can match it to someone who clicked your ad. These details improve matching. Look at the cards. The click I D, such as the f b c value made from f b c l i d. The browser I D, such as the f b p value. Hashed contact data, an email or phone that's scrambled, sent with consent. And the event time, when it actually happened. Send personal data only with consent, and as the platform's rules require.

steps.p: If your pixel and your server both send the same registration, the platform could count it twice. Deduplication means sending a shared event ID so the platform knows they are the same event.
steps.say: Here's a problem. If your pixel and your server both send the same registration, the platform could count it twice. Deduplication fixes that. You send a shared event I D, so the platform knows they're the same event. Same event, same I D. That's how deduplication works.

steps.p: Example: one person registers. The pixel and the server both report it with the same event name and the same event ID. The platform keeps one and drops the duplicate.
steps.say: Here's a worked example. One person registers. Look at the table. The browser pixel sends Complete Registration with an event I D. The server sends Complete Registration with the same event I D. The platform counts the first one and drops the second as a duplicate. One person, one registration, counted once.

steps.p: Hashed data is still personal data. Only collect and send what your privacy notice covers and what the person agreed to. The Compliance and safety module covers privacy and consent in detail.

d.text: Never send personal data you were not allowed to collect, even hashed. Follow privacy law and platform terms.

steps.say: Privacy comes first. Hashed data is still personal data. Only collect and send what your privacy notice covers, and what the person agreed to. The Compliance and safety module covers privacy and consent in detail. Read the warning: never send personal data you weren't allowed to collect, even hashed. Follow privacy law and platform terms.

steps.p: Run these checks after every install or page change. Most platforms have a test events tool that shows events arriving live. Its name and location change, so look in the current events manager.
d: Events show in the test tool
Only one pixel per platform per page
Each event fires once, not twice
The right event on the right page
Server and pixel share event IDs
steps.say: Run these checks after every install or page change. Events show in the test tool. Only one pixel per platform per page. Each event fires once, not twice. The right event on the right page. And server and pixel share event I Ds. Most platforms have a test events tool that shows events arriving live. Its name and location change, so look in the current events manager.

steps.p: The test events tool shows events from your own visit in real time. Open your page through it, tap the button, then watch the events land. We are not certain of current tab names; look for test events in Events Manager.
steps.say: Here's the test events tool, which shows events from your own visit in real time. Enter your page, open it through the tool, tap the button, then watch the events land. Look at the table in this example. Page View from the browser, received. Complete Registration from the browser, received. Complete Registration from the server, deduplicated. One sign-up, counted once. We're not certain of the current tab names, so look for test events in Events Manager.

steps.p: Pixel mistakes rarely stop your ads. They quietly feed the platform wrong signals, so it learns from the wrong people. Check for these after every install and every page change.

a.title: Mistake
items: Pixel and server with no shared ID
Optimising for FTDs at $20 a day

b.title: Fix
items: One pixel per platform per page
Fire on the real action only

steps.say: Pixel mistakes rarely stop your ads. They quietly feed the platform wrong signals, so it learns from the wrong people. Look at the mistakes and fixes. Two pixels on one page: one pixel per platform per page. Lead firing on page load: fire on the real action only. Pixel and server with no shared I D: the same event I D from both. Optimising for F T Ds at twenty dollars a day: use a shallower event until volume grows.

takeaways: A pixel reports events from the browser. CAPI reports them from a server.
Feed the deepest event that still has enough volume to learn.
Use a shared event ID so the same conversion is counted once.

A recorded action such as PageView, Lead, CompleteRegistration or Purchase.
A way for your server to send events directly to an ad platform without relying on the browser.
Making sure the same conversion sent by pixel and server is only counted once, using a shared event ID.

quiz.q: Where does a browser pixel run?
options: In the visitor's browser on your page
quiz.why: A pixel is code that runs in the visitor's browser when they load your page, which is why blockers can stop it.

quiz.q: Budget $140 a week, cost per registration $4. About how many registrations per week?
quiz.why: $140 ÷ $4 = 35 registrations a week.

quiz.q: Why do affiliates use server events for deposits?
options: Deposits happen off-site, often days later, where your pixel cannot see them
Server events are free and pixels are paid
Pixels are banned on landing pages
Server events make ads cheaper by default
quiz.why: Deposits happen on the advertiser's site. A postback brings them to your tool, which can send them to the platform as server events.

quiz.q: Pixel and server both send a registration with event ID reg_501. What happens?
quiz.why: A matching event name and event ID lets the platform deduplicate and keep one.

quiz.q: Which statement about hashed email is correct?
options: Hashed data is no longer personal data
It is still personal data and needs consent and a lawful basis
Hashing is only needed on TikTok
You can send any email list once it is hashed

lessons.say_intro: In this lesson you'll learn what a pixel does, how the Conversions A P I sends events from your server instead of the browser, and how deduplication makes sure each conversion is counted once.
lessons.say_outro: You've learned that a pixel reports browser events, the Conversions A P I sends events from your server, and a shared event I D stops double counting. Your task: open your ad platform's events manager, find the test events tool, load your landing page and confirm a Page View arrives. Now take the quiz.

lessons.title: Postbacks: the network reports back
objectives: By the end you can explain what a postback is and why affiliates use it.
By the end you can read a postback URL and its macros.
By the end you can test a postback and diagnose common problems.

steps.p: When a conversion happens at the advertiser, the network's server sends a web request to an address you gave it. That request is called a postback. It is also called server-to-server, or S2S, tracking.

d.s: The network calls your URL when someone converts

steps.say: When a conversion happens at the advertiser, the network's server sends a web request to an address you gave it. That request is called a postback. It's also called server to server, or S 2 S, tracking. In short, the network calls your URL when someone converts.

steps.p: The click ID you passed in the offer link is the thread that ties everything together. The network stores it at sign-up and sends it back with every conversion.
steps.say: Here's how a postback works. Follow the flow. A click arrives with your I D. The network stores the I D. The user registers or deposits. The network fires the postback. And your tool records it. The click I D you passed in the offer link is the thread that ties everything together. The network stores it at sign-up, and sends it back with every conversion.

steps.p: Example postback URL: track.example.com/pb?cid={sub1}&event={goal}&payout={payout}. Your tracker gives you the base receiving address. The network fills in the values in curly brackets each time a conversion fires.
steps.say: Let's take a postback URL apart. Look at the table. The base address is your tracker's receiver, and your tracker gives you that. Then come the parts in curly brackets. The c i d part carries the click I D you sent. The event part says what happened, like an F T D, a first time deposit. And the payout part says what it paid, like forty. Each time a conversion fires, the network fills in the values in curly brackets.

steps.p: The words in curly brackets are macros. The network swaps each one for the real value at the moment it fires. Every network names its macros differently.

d.text: Copy macro names from your network's documentation or manager. Never guess them. A wrong macro sends the literal text {sub1} instead of the ID.

steps.say: The words in curly brackets are called macros. They're placeholders. The network swaps each one for the real value at the moment it fires, and every network names its macros differently. So here's the tip on screen. Copy macro names from your network's documentation or manager. Never guess them. A wrong macro sends the literal placeholder text instead of the I D.

steps.h: A postback URL, ready to paste
steps.p: This is what you paste into the network panel. Your tracker gives you the start of the address. The network fills in each macro when it fires. The macro names here are examples only; your network will have its own.

d.note: Example macros. Copy the real names from your network's documentation.

steps.say: This is what you paste into the network panel, shown on screen. Your tracker gives you the start of the address. Then come the click I D, the event, the payout and the status, each as a macro. The network fills in each macro when it fires. The macro names here are examples only. Your network will have its own, so copy the real names from its documentation.

steps.p: Depending on the offer and network, you may get one postback or several for the same user. Ask your affiliate manager which events they fire and what each one means.
steps.say: Depending on the offer and network, you may get one postback or several for the same user. Look at the cards. Registration, the user signed up. F T D, first deposit made. Qualified F T D, it met the payout rules. Deposit or revenue, for RevShare deals. And rejection, a conversion reversed. Ask your affiliate manager which events they fire, and what each one means.

steps.h: Pixel on the offer page versus postback
steps.p: Some beginners ask to put their pixel on the advertiser's site. Most advertisers will not allow it, and even when they do, it misses deposits that happen later. Postbacks are the standard way.
steps.say: Some beginners ask to put their pixel on the advertiser's site. Compare the two sides. Your pixel on their site is usually not allowed. It's browser-based and easy to block, misses later deposits and is hard to tie to payouts. A postback is standard for networks. It's server-based, fires whenever the deposit happens, and carries the payout value. Even when advertisers allow a pixel, it misses deposits that happen later. That's why postbacks are the standard way.

steps.h: From postback to the ad platform
steps.p: A postback alone only updates your tracker. To help the ad platform learn, your tool turns the postback into a server event, using the click data saved when the user first clicked.
steps.say: A postback alone only updates your tracker. To help the ad platform learn, there's one more step. Follow the flow. The network postback goes to your tracker or tool. Your tool turns it into a server event to Meta, using the click data saved when the user first clicked. And Meta learns from F T Ds.

steps.h: Worked example: a week of postbacks
steps.p: Example: over seven days you send 1,500 clicks. Postbacks report 120 registrations and 14 FTDs. The network later marks 10 of them as qualified under the offer rules.
steps.more: Example figures. A qualified FTD is one that meets the offer's rules, such as a minimum deposit amount or a check that the user is real and in an allowed country. Only qualified FTDs are paid on many CPA deals. That is why you track both: FTDs tell you about your traffic, qualified FTDs tell you about your income.
steps.say: Here's a week of postbacks, with example figures. Over seven days you send one thousand five hundred clicks. Postbacks report one hundred and twenty registrations and fourteen F T Ds. Later, the network marks ten of them as qualified under the offer rules. A qualified F T D meets those rules, such as a minimum deposit, or a check that the user is real and in an allowed country. On many C P A deals, cost per acquisition deals, only qualified F T Ds are paid. F T Ds tell you about your traffic. Qualified F T Ds tell you about your income.

steps.p: Example: 10 qualified FTDs at a $40 payout. Postbacks that carry the payout value let your tracker do this sum for you, per ad set, every hour.
steps.say: Now the revenue. Look at the equation. Ten qualified F T Ds, times a forty dollar payout, equals four hundred dollars revenue. That's an example. Postbacks that carry the payout value let your tracker do this sum for you, per ad set, every hour.

steps.p: Example: you spent $300 on those 1,500 clicks and earned $400. ROI is profit divided by spend: ($400 minus $300) ÷ $300 = 0.333, so about 33%.
steps.say: And the return on the test. In this example, you spent three hundred dollars on those one thousand five hundred clicks, and earned four hundred. R O I, return on investment, is profit divided by spend. So four hundred minus three hundred, divided by three hundred, is about thirty three percent. That's the number on screen, thirty three point three. It's an example, not a benchmark.

steps.p: Never assume a postback works. Many networks offer a test conversion button, or your manager can fire one for you. Check each line before real money goes in.
d: Postback URL saved in the network
Click ID matches a real click
steps.say: Never assume a postback works. Many networks offer a test conversion button, or your manager can fire one for you. Before real money goes in, check each line. The postback URL is saved in the network. A test conversion was fired. The conversion shows in your tracker. The click I D matches a real click. And the payout value is correct.

steps.h: Walkthrough: add and test a postback
steps.p: Network panels differ, but the steps are the same idea everywhere. We are not certain of any network's current menu names; if you cannot find the postback settings, ask your affiliate manager.

steps.title: Open postback settings
steps.text: In the network panel, find postbacks, often under tools, settings or the offer page.

steps.title: Fire a test conversion
steps.text: Use the test button, or ask your manager to fire one, with a made-up click ID you will recognise.

steps.title: Find it in your tracker
steps.text: Open your tracker or receiving log. The test should show your click ID, the event and the payout.

blocks.value: Example. A literal {sub1} here means a wrong macro.

steps.say: Here's how to add and test a postback. Tap Next to follow each step. First, in the network panel, find postbacks, often under tools, settings or the offer page. Choose the offer and event, paste your postback URL and save. Second, fire a test conversion. Use the test button, or ask your manager, with a made-up click I D you'll recognise. Third, find it in your tracker or receiving log. It should show your click I D, the event and the payout. If you see the literal macro text there, the macro is wrong. steps.p: A deposit can happen hours or days after a click, so its postback arrives late too. Judging an ad set on FTDs a few hours after launch will mislead you. The Budget and kill rules module turns this into a matured-spend rule.

d.text: Give FTD postbacks time to arrive before you kill an ad set. Judge only spend old enough for its FTDs to have arrived, and use registrations as the early signal.

Read the warning. Give F T D postbacks time to arrive before you kill an ad set. Judge only spend old enough for its F T Ds to have arrived, and use registrations as the early signal. The Budget and kill rules module turns this into a matured-spend rule.

steps.p: Most postback problems come from a few simple setup mistakes. When numbers look wrong, check this list first, before you blame the network or the ad platform.

rows: Network shows FTDs, tracker shows none
Postback not set or wrong URL
Click ID not passed in sub ID

steps.say: When numbers look wrong, check this table before you blame anyone. Network shows F T Ds but the tracker shows none: the postback isn't set, or the URL is wrong. Conversions with an empty click I D: the click I D wasn't passed in the sub ID. Every conversion counted twice: the postback was added twice. Payout always zero: the payout macro is missing or wrong. And the literal macro text in reports: the macro name is wrong.

steps.p: The table above lists symptoms. These are the habits behind them. Avoid these four habits and most postback problems never happen, which means you never have to rebuild a week of data from screenshots.
d: Guessing macro names|copy them from the docs
Adding the postback twice|one postback per event
Judging FTDs too soon|wait for matured spend
No test before spend|fire a test conversion first
steps.say: The table showed symptoms. These cards show the habits behind them. Guessing macro names: copy them from the docs. Adding the postback twice: one postback per event. Judging F T Ds too soon: wait for matured spend. No test before spend: fire a test conversion first. Avoid these four habits, and most postback problems never happen. You'll never have to rebuild a week of data from screenshots.

steps.h: Compliance: what a postback should carry
steps.p: A postback needs your click ID, the event and the payout. It does not need the user's name, phone or email. For trading and gambling offers the advertiser holds identity checks and that data should stay with them.

d.text: Never ask a network to send personal data in postbacks. If one arrives, stop storing it and tell your manager.

steps.say: A postback needs your click I D, the event and the payout. It doesn't need the user's name, phone or email. For trading and gambling offers, the advertiser holds identity checks, and that data should stay with them. Read the warning. Never ask a network to send personal data in postbacks. If one arrives, stop storing it and tell your manager.

The click ID you pass in the offer link is what ties it back to your ad.
Test with a test conversion first and give FTD postbacks time to arrive.

options: A pixel on the advertiser's page
A request the network's server sends to your tool when a conversion happens
A message the user posts back to your ad
An email report sent each morning

lessons.say_intro: This lesson covers postbacks, the way a network reports conversions back to you, server to server. You'll learn to read a postback URL and its macros, and how to test one before you spend.

lessons.title: Attribution and your minimum setup
objectives: By the end you can explain attribution windows in plain words.
By the end you can list the main reasons platform and network numbers differ.
By the end you can set up and run a minimum tracking system with a daily sheet.

steps.h: Attribution means who gets the credit
steps.p: Attribution is the set of rules that decides which ad gets credit for a conversion. A person might see three ads and click one, then deposit four days later. The rules decide which ad, if any, is credited.
steps.say: Attribution is the set of rules that decides which ad gets credit for a conversion. A person might see three ads, click one, then deposit four days later. The rules decide which ad, if any, gets the credit. And every tool uses its own rules.

steps.h: The parts of an attribution window
steps.p: An attribution window is how long after a click or a view a conversion can still be credited to an ad. Each platform sets its own windows and some let you change them.
d: Click window|days after a click that still count
View window|days after only seeing the ad
Conversion time|when the action actually happened
Report time|when it shows in your dashboard
steps.say: An attribution window is how long after a click or a view a conversion can still be credited to an ad. Look at the cards. The click window is the days after a click that still count. The view window is the days after only seeing the ad. Conversion time is when the action actually happened. And report time is when it shows in your dashboard. Each platform sets its own windows, and some let you change them.

steps.p: At the time of writing, a common Meta default is a 7-day click and 1-day view window. We are not certain this is still the default for your account, and names change, so check the current Ads Manager before you compare reports.

d.text: Write the attribution setting you used next to every report you save, so you compare like with like.

steps.say: Defaults change. At the time of writing, a common Meta default is a seven day click and one day view window. We're not certain that's still the default for your account, and names change, so check the current Ads Manager before you compare reports. And here's the tip: write the attribution setting you used next to every report you save, so you compare like with like.

steps.say: In Meta's reporting, you can usually show the attribution setting as a column. Look at this example screen. steps.say: Platforms and networks count differently, so a gap is normal. Look at the reasons. Different windows: one counts day nine, one doesn't. View-through credit for people who never clicked. Time zones, so a conversion lands on different days. Blocked tracking, so some browser events never arrive. Modelled conversions, where the platform estimates what it can't see. Qualification, where the network rejects some. And bots and duplicates inflating one side. Your job is to know the reasons, keep the gap steady, and notice when it suddenly changes.

steps.p: Example: Meta shows 18 registrations for yesterday. The network shows 14. The gap is 4, which is 4 ÷ 18 = about 22% fewer on the network side.

d.text: Pay attention to the 14 for profit maths, because that is what the network counts. Use Meta's 18 to compare ad sets against each other, since the same rules apply to all of them.

steps.h: A gap to watch versus a gap to fix
steps.p: A small, steady gap is normal. A sudden change usually means something broke. Learn the difference so you do not panic over noise or ignore a real fault.

a.title: Normal, keep watching
items: Explained by windows or time zones

steps.say: A small, steady gap is normal. A sudden change usually means something broke. On the left, normal, keep watching: the gap is similar day after day, both sides move together, and it's explained by windows or time zones. On the right, broken, fix now: one side drops to zero, the gap suddenly doubles, or conversions arrive with no click I D. Learn the difference, so you don't panic over noise or ignore a real fault.

steps.h: Decision rules you apply to the sheet
steps.p: Example with a $40 payout and $30 target. These are the starting rules from the Budget and kill rules module; adapt them to your vertical and data. Check rows from the top and count only network-confirmed FTDs.

rows: Spend ≥ 3 × target, CPA over kill line

steps.more: The CPA kill line is the lower of 1.5 × target and break-even. Here 1.5 × $30 = $45, but the $40 payout is lower, so the line is $40. Scale steps are +20%, at least 48 hours apart. The full card, including Keep, is taught in the Budget and kill rules module.
steps.say: Here are the decision rules you apply to the sheet. Example: a forty dollar payout and a thirty dollar target. Check rows from the top, and count only network-confirmed F T Ds. Kill at zero F T Ds once spend reaches two times target, sixty dollars. Kill once spend reaches three times target, ninety dollars, if C P A, cost per acquisition, is over the kill line. That line is the lower of one point five times target and break-even, so forty dollars here. Scale twenty percent with three or more F T Ds at a C P A of twenty four dollars or less. Anything else, hold. These are starting rules, so adapt them.

quiz.q: What is an attribution window?
options: The hours your ads are allowed to run
The time after a click or view during which a conversion can be credited to an ad
The time a network takes to pay you
The size of your landing page
quiz.why: It is the credit period. Conversions outside it are not credited to the ad by that tool.

quiz.q: Meta shows 18 registrations and the network shows 14. Which do you use to calculate profit?
quiz.why: You are paid on the network's count, so profit maths uses the network number.

quiz.q: Which is a sign that tracking is broken, not just a normal gap?
options: The network side suddenly drops to zero
The gap is similar every day
Numbers differ by a few conversions
quiz.why: A sudden drop to zero or a sudden jump in the gap points to a fault. Steady small gaps are normal.

quiz.q: Daily sheet: ad set spent $20 and got 2 FTDs; another spent $20 and got 1. Total cost per FTD?
quiz.why: Total spend $40 ÷ total FTDs 3 = about $13.33.

quiz.q: Your postback was broken for one day. What should you do about that day's data?
options: Scale the ad sets that looked best that day
Fix the postback, then rebuild the day from the network report before deciding
Kill every ad set with zero FTDs that day
Ignore it, data always evens out
quiz.why: Decisions on broken data are guesses. Repair the setup and fill the gap from the network report first.

lessons.say_intro: In this lesson you'll learn what attribution windows are, why platform and network numbers never quite match, and how to run a simple minimum tracking setup with a daily sheet.
lessons.say_outro: You've learned how attribution windows work, why platform and network numbers differ, which one to use for money and which for comparisons, and how to run a minimum setup with a daily sheet. Your task: create your daily sheet with columns for date, ad set, spend, platform registrations, network registrations and F T Ds, and note your ad account time zone at the top. Now take the quiz.

exam.q: You spent $60 on a new ad set. Meta shows 9 registrations; the network shows 0 clicks from your sub IDs. What is the most likely problem?
options: The offer link is wrong or missing your sub IDs
exam.why: Zero clicks recorded by the network means traffic is not reaching the offer link with your IDs. Check the link before judging the offer.

exam.q: Target CPA $30. An ad set has spent $65. Meta reports 3 conversions, but the network confirms 0 FTDs for its sub ID after postbacks have had time to arrive. What do you do?
options: Hold it until Meta and the network agree
Kill it: spend is past 2 × target with 0 network-confirmed FTDs
Double the budget to get more data
exam.why: Decisions use network-confirmed conversions. $65 is past the $60 zero-conversion kill line (2 × $30), so the starting rule says kill.

exam.q: You put ad set names in sub3, but the network report groups everything under "(empty)". What happened?
options: The postback has the wrong payout macro
The attribution window is too short
The sub3 value is not reaching the network, so the link or placeholder is wrong
exam.why: An empty sub ID means the value never arrived in the offer link. Check the link and any dynamic placeholder.

exam.q: Your budget is $15 a day. Registrations cost about $3 and FTDs about $45. Which event is the more practical optimisation goal to start with?
exam.why: At $105 a week you get about 35 registrations but only about 2 FTDs. Registrations give the system far more to learn from, while link clicks and page views say little about value.

exam.q: Your pixel and server both send Lead for the same person but the platform counts two leads. What is the fix?
options: Change the event name on the server
Send the same event ID from both so they deduplicate
exam.why: Deduplication relies on the same event name and a shared event ID.

exam.q: Postback test: the tracker shows a conversion but payout reads 0. What do you check?
options: The payout macro in the postback URL
exam.why: A zero payout with a working postback usually means the payout macro is missing or misnamed.

exam.q: One week: 12 qualified FTDs at $35 payout, $360 spend. What is the ROI?
Meta and the network have differed by about 20% every day for two weeks. Today Meta shows 25 registrations and the network shows 3. What do you do?
options: Change the attribution window to match
Treat it as a likely tracking or traffic fault and investigate before deciding
exam.why: A steady gap is normal. A sudden jump from about 20% to nearly 90% points to a broken link, postback or junk traffic.

exam.q: A teammate wants to put your Meta pixel directly on the advertiser's deposit page. What is the better standard approach?
options: Ask the advertiser for their password
Use a postback from the network and send a server event from your tool
Copy the advertiser's page and host it yourself
exam.why: Advertisers rarely allow your pixel. Postbacks plus server events are the standard, honest way to get deposit data.

exam.q: A teammate wants to put each lead's phone number in sub2 so the network report shows who converted. What is the right answer?
options: Fine, as long as the numbers are hashed in a sheet later
No: keep personal data out of links and sub IDs; use a click ID instead
exam.why: Links and sub IDs end up in logs and reports. Platform terms and privacy law usually forbid personal data there. A click ID matches the conversion without exposing anyone.
